name: A Black Hole in a Universe Filled by a Scalar Field
description: Schwarzschild's black hole in a massless scalar field whose gradient far away points along one axis, the scalar counterpart of Ernst's black hole in Melvin's magnetic universe. Somasri Sen and Narayan Banerjee wrote the metric down in 2001, and Vitor Cardoso and José Natário found it again in 2024. The field is smooth on the horizon, and the curvature grows without bound far from the axis.
convention: The mass parameter $m = GM/c^2$ is a length and the gradient $b$ an inverse length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A black hole can sit inside a field that fills the whole universe [ernst1976b]. Frederick Ernst's does: his metric of 1976 places Schwarzschild's hole in Mael Melvin's magnetic universe, a bundle of parallel field lines held together by their own gravity [ernst1976b, melvin1964]. Far from the hole the field points along one axis, and the spacetime is not asymptotically flat [cardoso2025]. What becomes of the picture when the field is the plainest kind of matter, a massless scalar field?¶A black hole alone in a universe that flattens out far away cannot carry a nontrivial massless scalar field that is smooth on its horizon, by the no-hair theorems of J. E. Chase and Jacob Bekenstein [chase1970, bekenstein1972, herdeiro2025]. Somasri Sen and Narayan Banerjee put that rule to the test on the charged, spinning hole of Kerr and Newman, which they dressed with a scalar field by a procedure close to that of A. Eriş and Metin Gürses from 1977 [sen2001, eris1977]. Two of their solutions turned the would-be horizon into a singularity, and the third, a field growing along the axis as $(r - m)\cos\theta$, left it regular [sen2001]. They judged that it "could not really be considered as a serious counter example due to its pathological behaviour at $r \rightarrow \infty$", where the spacetime is not asymptotically flat and the field grows without bound [sen2001]. Without spin or charge, their third solution of 2001 is Schwarzschild's hole in a universe filled by a scalar field [sen2001].¶The same metric came back in October 2024, when Vitor Cardoso and José Natário went looking for a scalar counterpart of Ernst's hole [cardoso2025]. They started from Hans Buchdahl's static solutions with a scalar field, from 1959, and with the field growing linearly along the axis the metric is free of $z$ only if a clock at rest ticks at the same rate everywhere [cardoso2025, buchdahl1959reciprocal]. That is their scalar counterpart of Melvin's universe, $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + e^{-b^2\rho^2}(d\rho^2 + dz^2) + \rho^2d\phi^2$, in which the gradient of the field is least on the axis and grows as $e^{b^2\rho^2/2}$ away from it [cardoso2025]. Spatial infinity lies a finite distance from the axis and light gets there in a finite time, so the universe is not globally hyperbolic [cardoso2025]. Following Ernst's lead, and "after some experimenting", they then put Schwarzschild's hole inside it [cardoso2025].¶Thirteen days later Carlos Herdeiro showed that the solution belongs to a family built on Hermann Weyl's construction of 1917 [herdeiro2025, weyl1917]. In Weyl's coordinates a static, axisymmetric metric with a massless scalar field is fixed by two harmonic functions in a flat space of three dimensions, one for gravity and one for the field, and the two add their parts to the last metric function independently [herdeiro2025]. Schwarzschild's hole is the potential of a rod of length $2m$ on the axis, and the field $\varphi \propto z$ is a growing dipole laid over it [herdeiro2025]. The field changes Weyl's second function by $-b^2\rho^2/2$ and leaves the first alone [herdeiro2025]. The surface gravity of the horizon, which Yen-Kheng Lim worked out in 2026, is Schwarzschild's, $c^2/4m$, whatever the strength of the field [lim2026].¶Is the scalar universe as tame as Melvin's? Herdeiro found that it is not: away from the axis the curvature grows without bound as $r \to \infty$, light reaches that edge after a finite affine distance, and no horizon hides it [herdeiro2025]. Out along the equator $F$ falls away as a Gaussian, and a ray of light from near the hole reaches $r \to \infty$ within a finite coordinate time [lim2026]. Lim drew the causal structure as a Kruskal diagram whose far edges are timelike singularities [lim2026]. On the axis $F = 1$, and along it the metric is Schwarzschild's, $-(1 - 2m/r)c^2dt^2 + dr^2/(1 - 2m/r)$ [cardoso2025]. Light has a single circular orbit, the ring $r = 3m$ in the equatorial plane [herdeiro2025].¶Cristian Stelea, Marina-Aura Dariescu, and Vitalie Lungu set the hole accelerating, spinning, and charged in 2025, and pointed out that the spinning version was already among Sen and Banerjee's solutions [stelea2025]. Melvin's magnetic field went back on top of the scalar one with José Barrientos, Fabrizio Canfora, Adolfo Cisterna, Keanu Müller, and Anibal Neira in 2026, so that a single hole sits in both [barrientos2026]. Cardoso and Natário suggest the spacetime may be "especially appealing in the context of dark matter models with a scalar or axionic degree of freedom" [cardoso2025]. Herdeiro reads it as "a proxy to explore scalar-BH interactions" near the hole, "possibly considering a large distance cut-off to remove the singularity at infinity" [herdeiro2025].

related.text: Switch the field off, $b = 0$, and the metric is Schwarzschild's, with $r_s = 2m$.
Ernst's black hole in Melvin's magnetic universe, whose scalar twin this is. Cardoso and Natário built the scalar universe and its black hole after Melvin's and Ernst's [cardoso2025].
Schwarzschild's hole with a scalar field that dies away with distance, which turns the horizon into a singularity. A field that grows along the axis leaves it regular [sen2001, herdeiro2025].
Schwarzschild's rod of Weyl's class with a growing quadrupole of distant matter laid over it, in a vacuum. Here the growing term is a dipole of a scalar field [herdeiro2025].

coordinates.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass of the black hole

Gradient of the scalar field far out along the axis, an inverse length; the field is $\varphi = \sqrt{c^4/4\pi G}\,b\left(r - m\right)\cos\theta$, with $R_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi$, and $b = 0$ is Schwarzschild's metric
The factor that shrinks distances along $r$ and $\theta$, equal to 1 on the axis and on the horizon

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Somasri Sen and Narayan Banerjee and of Vitor Cardoso and José Natário, Schwarzschild's at $b = 0$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Weyl

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass of the black hole

Gradient of the scalar field, an inverse length; the field is $\varphi = \sqrt{c^4/4\pi G}\,bz$, with $R_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi$, and $b = 0$ is Schwarzschild's metric
The prolate spheroidal radial coordinate, half the sum of the distances from the two ends of the rod $\rho = 0$, $|z| \le m$, over $m$
The prolate spheroidal angular coordinate, half the difference of the same two distances, over $m$
Weyl's first function, the potential of Schwarzschild's rod; it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_\rho^2\psi + \dfrac{1}{\rho}\partial_\rho\psi + \partial_z^2\psi = 0$

Weyl's second function, fixed by $\psi$ and the field through $\partial_\rho\gamma = \rho\left(\left(\partial_\rho\psi\right)^2 - \left(\partial_z\psi\right)^2 - b^2\right)$ and $\partial_z\gamma = 2\rho\,\partial_\rho\psi\,\partial_z\psi$; the term $-b^2\rho^2/2$ is the field's

coordinates.convention: We use Weyl's canonical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths; the horizon is the rod $\rho = 0$, $|z| \le m$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.convention: We use cylindrical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$ about the axis the field points along, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths, for the universe with no black hole, $m = 0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
